title: Bible Verses for Grief and Loss | Prayed
headline: Bible verses for grief, for the weeks after
dek: Fourteen verses for mourning, arranged for the first days, the long middle, and the hope that only makes sense later. Nothing here will tell you to feel better.
desc: Fourteen Bible verses for grief from the World English Bible, arranged for the first days after a loss, the long middle, and the hope that only makes sense later. With a short prayer to write for each stage.
card: Fourteen verses for mourning, arranged for the first days, the long middle, and the hope that comes later.
intro: Grief does not want verses. In the first days it does not want anything, and well-meaning people who arrive with scripture ready are often the hardest to bear. So a page of Bible verses for grief needs to begin by saying what it is not. It is not a set of things that will make you feel better. It is not an argument that you should.

What it is: the words people have brought to God when someone died, for a very long time, quoted here exactly as they appear in the World English Bible. They are arranged in the order grief tends to move, not because it moves in order, but because the verse that is unbearable in the first week can be the one you need in the sixth month.
Read only as far as you can. The rest will still be here.

paras: These verses do not explain anything. They say that God is close to the broken and that mourning is not a failure of faith. That is all the first days can hold.

verses.note: Near. Not fixing, not explaining. Near. It is the only promise that makes sense in the first week.
Jesus calls the mourners blessed, which is not the same as calling them fine. The comfort is promised, not scheduled.
Binds up is a slow verb. Wounds are dressed, not erased.
From a book that is entirely a lament. It does not deny that God causes grief. It says compassion is on the other side of it.

sections.pray: I do not have words. I am just going to sit here and let you be near, because you said you would be. I am not asking for anything yet.

paras: After the casseroles stop and the calls thin out, grief becomes ordinary, and that is its own kind of hard. These are the verses for the months when nobody is checking on you anymore and the loss is simply the shape of your days.

verses.note: Through. The valley has another side, even when you cannot see it from where you are standing.
The comfort you receive is meant to become the comfort you give. That is not a job for now. It is a reason, later, that this was not wasted.
Weeping may stay for the night. The psalmist does not say how long the night is.
Garland for ashes, oil for mourning. An exchange, not a denial. The ashes are real and so is what replaces them.

sections.pray: It has been months and it is still the first thing I think of. Everyone else has moved on. Walk this part with me, the part where no one is watching. Turn the ashes into something eventually. I cannot see how.

paras: These verses are about resurrection and the end of death. In the first week they can sound like a change of subject. Later, they are the only subject. Read them when you are ready and not before.

verses.note: Said to Martha at her brother's tomb, before the miracle, while she was still angry with him for being late. Jesus does not correct the grief. He answers it.
Grieve, Paul says, just not like people with no hope. The grief is assumed. The hope is what is added.
Troubled is the honest word. The verse does not say the heart will not be troubled. It says do not let it stay that way alone.
Precious. Whatever else that death was, it was not overlooked.
Every tear. Death no more. This is the end of the story, and it is a promise, not a metaphor.

sections.pray: I believe you are the resurrection. I do not feel it today. Hold the belief for me until I can hold it again, and keep the promise about the tears. I am counting on that one.

closing: One of the strange gifts of grief is that it teaches you to pray honestly, and one of its cruelties is that you forget those prayers. The thing you said to God at three in the morning in the second week is gone by the second month, and with it the evidence that you were met there.

Writing them down keeps them. Prayed brings each written prayer back to you at three days, a week, a month, six months and a year, which means the prayer from the first week is placed in front of you again in the long middle, when you need to see that you survived it. You can tag the person's name and every prayer for them gathers in one place, from the first day to whatever comes later. Nothing you write leaves your phone.
There is no right pace for any of this. Write when you can. Let it come back when it does.
